html:
The treaty signed in Rome on 25 March 1957 by six countries, Belgium, France, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and West Germany, which founded the European Economic Community (EEC), the common market at the core of today's European Union.

The six had already pooled their coal and steel industries in the European Coal and Steel Community in 1951. The idea, pushed by men such as Jean Monnet, was to tie former enemies so closely that war between them would be impossible.

The treaty, in force from 1 January 1958, set up:

  • a customs union, with no tariffs inside and a common tariff outside;
  • free movement of goods, workers, services and capital;
  • common policies, above all the Common Agricultural Policy;
  • the institutions: the Commission, the Council, an assembly and a court.

A second treaty signed the same day created Euratom for nuclear energy. The EEC grew to include Britain, Denmark and Ireland in 1973 and became the European Union in 1993. The Treaty of Rome, much amended, is still one of the EU's two founding treaties.
sum: The treaty signed in Rome on 25 March 1957 by six countries, Belgium, France, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and West Germany, which founded the European Economic Community (EEC), the common market at the core of today's European Union.
